beats.narration_text: Bonjour. This is Liam, in for Bear, with a short film for INFO seventy-three seventy-five, Computational Skepticism for AI. You might think checking an answer is cheaper than making one. In mathematics it often is. When a model makes the answer, it runs the other way: making is cheap, and checking is the expensive part.

backspaces 'cheaper than making one' -> 'still cheaper when a model makes one' on the spoken correction

beats.narration_text: Four terms. Verify: check an output against the world, not against the output. Asymmetry: when making and checking cost different amounts. System of record: the store that holds the actual state. And budget: the time and people you set aside to verify.

terms.meaning: check an output against the world, not the output
making and checking cost different amounts
the store that holds the actual state
the time and people set aside to verify

qc.sparse_reason: TERMS card: four prerequisites, one line each.

beats.narration_text: Start with a piece of computer-science folklore, and it's true. Hand someone a very large number and ask for its factors: that is hard. Hand them the factors and ask them to multiply: that is easy, and the check is done. Most of cryptography is built on this asymmetry. Solving is dear. Verifying is cheap.

shot.visual_intent: A kraft crate ('big number') on the left; the cost meter's 'solve' bar creeps out long while two small factor tiles emerge ('factors'); then the tiles multiply back: the 'verify' bar is a short stub and an ink check lands at once.

show.event: factoring: the solve bar grows long
multiplying back: the verify bar is a stub, a check lands

shot.motion_claim: A kraft crate ('big number') on the left; the cost meter's 'solve' bar creeps out long while two small factor tiles emerge ('factors'); then the tiles multiply back: the 'verify' bar is a short stub and an ink check lands at once.

beats.narration_text: Now put a model in the picture. The asymmetry inverts. Producing the output is cheap. The model runs, the result appears, and in the chapter's numbers the latency is milliseconds and the cost is fractions of a cent. The solve bar barely moves.

shot.visual_intent: The dark model block arrives ('model'); a white output slip pops out of it in one blink ('output'); the cost meter's 'solve' bar is a sliver; the 'verify' bar waits, empty.
shot.motion_claim: The dark model block arrives ('model'); a white output slip pops out of it in one blink ('output'); the cost meter's 'solve' bar is a sliver; the 'verify' bar waits, empty.

beats.narration_text: Verifying it is expensive. Take the chapter's triage score. To check it, you need a clinician, with twenty minutes, a stethoscope, and a body of training the model does not have. The verify bar keeps growing.

shot.visual_intent: The output slip sits beside a kraft patient peg on a chair ('patient'); a clinician peg walks in ('clinician'); a clock wedge fills beside them while the 'verify' bar grows long; a check lands only at the end.

show.event: the clock fills; the verify bar grows

shot.motion_claim: The output slip sits beside a kraft patient peg on a chair ('patient'); a clinician peg walks in ('clinician'); a clock wedge fills beside them while the 'verify' bar grows long; a check lands only at the end.

beats.narration_text: Or take an agent's report that an email was deleted. To verify it, you query the provider's servers, examine the actual data state, and compare it with what the agent claimed. In the chapter's numbers, the output cost a fraction of a cent. The verification costs an hour of senior labor.

shot.visual_intent: The model block with its report slip ('report'); a server stack on the right ('system of record'); a human peg draws a query line to the server, its lights come on, a record page comes back beside the report ('compare'); the 'verify' bar grows long.
shot.motion_claim: The model block with its report slip ('report'); a server stack on the right ('system of record'); a human peg draws a query line to the server, its lights come on, a record page comes back beside the report ('compare'); the 'verify' bar grows long.

beats.narration_text: This is not a complaint. It is an observation about where the costs sit, and where they will keep sitting for the foreseeable future. Side by side: with a proof, verifying is the short bar. With a deployed model, it is the long one. The bars compare kinds of work, not measured costs.

shot.visual_intent: Two cost meters side by side: 'proof' (solve long, verify short) and 'model' (solve short, verify long), labelled 'illustrative'; a time arrow draws under the model's meter and the same pair repeats along it.

show.event: the pair repeats along the time arrow

shot.motion_claim: Two cost meters side by side: 'proof' (solve long, verify short) and 'model' (solve short, verify long), labelled 'illustrative'; a time arrow draws under the model's meter and the same pair repeats along it.

beats.narration_text: If you do not budget for verification, you will not get verification. The system produces outputs at scale. Verification does not happen at scale. A small budget checks a few. The rest go out unchecked, and every one of them looks like a success.

shot.visual_intent: The model streams slips into a grid; a short 'budget' bar beside a human peg; the peg marks two slips with a terracotta dot ('verified'); every slip in the grid carries an ink check regardless ('looks right').

show.event: the budget bar is short; two get verified

shot.motion_claim: The model streams slips into a grid; a short 'budget' bar beside a human peg; the peg marks two slips with a terracotta dot ('verified'); every slip in the grid carries an ink check regardless ('looks right').

beats.narration_text: They stay indistinguishable. Until one of them is the patient, or the loan, or the warrant, or the email that did not actually get deleted. Under the check it was carrying, that one was wrong the whole time.

shot.visual_intent: The same grid of checked slips; one slip lifts and turns over; an ink cross is on its underside ('wrong'); the others keep their checks ('looked the same').
shot.motion_claim: The same grid of checked slips; one slip lifts and turns over; an ink cross is on its underside ('wrong'); the others keep their checks ('looked the same').

beats.narration_text: So automate the verification? That is the wrong fix. A checker that is another model has the same problem, sitting one layer up. Its verdict is cheap to produce and just as expensive to verify. Same shape, one layer up.

shot.visual_intent: A second dark block of the same shape drops onto the model ('checker'); it emits a check slip; a second cost meter appears beside it with the same shape as the first ('same shape').

show.event: the checker lands on the model
its meter has the same shape

shot.motion_claim: A second dark block of the same shape drops onto the model ('checker'); it emits a check slip; a second cost meter appears beside it with the same shape as the first ('same shape').

beats.narration_text: The right fix is design. Build the system so that the verification a human can perform tells you what you need to know. One human check, placed where it counts: at the system of record, not at the report. That is the check you budget for, and the one that is cheap enough to scale.

shot.visual_intent: The model and its report slip; the server stack ('system of record'); a human peg's check line aims at the report first and an ink cross fades over it ('not the report'), then swings to the server, whose lights come on and a check lands ('one check'); the 'verify' bar is short.

show.event: not the report: the line swings to the server

shot.motion_claim: The model and its report slip; the server stack ('system of record'); a human peg's check line aims at the report first and an ink cross fades over it ('not the report'), then swings to the server, whose lights come on and a check lands ('one check'); the 'verify' bar is short.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take one AI output you act on, and paste this into Claude: Here is one AI output I act on: describe it. Help me price it honestly: what it cost to produce, and what it would cost to actually verify against the world, in time and in who has to do it. Then name the one check a human could do in five minutes that would tell me the most, and say whether it checks the world or only the report. Then check two things yourself. Did you price the verification honestly, in time and in people? And is your five-minute check against the world, or only against the report?
